document.abstract: Japan Broadcasting Corporation (NHK) has been researching and developing Super Hi-Vision, the 7680 × 4320-pixel (UHDTV2) version of ultrahigh-definition television, for future broadcasting. Last year, NHK and Shizuoka University as a collaborative work, developed a complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) image sensor with 120 frame/sec, 33 megapixels, and a 12-bit analog-to-digital converter in conformance to the highest resolution and frame frequency specified in the Recommendation of the International Telecommunications Union Recommendations Section, broadcasting service (television) series 2020. NHK also developed a 120 frame/sec 3-chip color camera equipped with this image sensor. In this paper, NHK \recently developed a 120 frame/sec 33-megapixel single-chip color CMOS image sensor and a compact UHDTV2 camera head equipped with this image sensor. Because the width, height, and depth are about 5, 5, and 6-in., respectively, and it weighs only 4.5 lbs, it was significantly smaller and lighter than conventional UHDTV2 cameras. The optical size of the image sensor is 25mm in its diameter, and the camera head is compatible with super 35mm PL(positive-lock mount lenses for various cameras for digital cinema.

authors.bio: Hiroshi Shimamoto received a B.E. degree in electronic engineering from Chiba University in 1989 and M.E. and Ph.D. degrees in information processing from Tokyo Institute of Technology in 1991 and 2008, respectively. In 1991, he joined NHK (Japan Broadcasting Corp.). Since 1993, he has been working on research and development of UHDTV (ultrahigh-definition TV) cameras and image sensors at the NHK Science & Technology Research Laboratories. From 2005 to 2006, Shimamoto was a visiting scholar at Stanford University. He is a member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE).
authors.name: Hiroshi Shimamoto

authors.bio: Toshio Yasue has been researching CMOS image sensors and camera systems at the Science and Technology Research Laboratories of NHK. He received a ME degree in applied physics from the University of Tokyo in 2008.
authors.name: Toshio Yasue

authors.bio: Kazuya Kitamura received B.E. and M.E. degrees from Chiba University in 1998 and 2000, respectively. In 2000, he joined NHK. From 2000 to 2003, he worked at the Fukuoka regional broadcasting station as a television engineer. Since 2003, he has been engaged in the research and development of ultra-high-speed CCD and ultra-high-definition CMOS image sensors with high frame rate in the Science and Technology Research Laboratories.
authors.name: Kazuya Kitamura

authors.bio: Toshihisa Watabe received B.E. and M.E. degrees in electrical engineering from Keio University, Yokohama, Japan, in 1989 and 1991, respectively. In 1991, he joined NHK, Tokyo, and worked at the Niigata regional broadcasting station from 1991 to 1994. Since 1994, he has been with NHK STRL, where he has been engaged in the research and development of highly-sensitive image sensors with HARP target and field emitter array, advanced image sensors with organic films, and ultra-high-definition CMOS image sensors with high frame rate. Since 2012, he has been sent on loan to NHK Engineering System, Inc.
authors.name: Toshihisa Watabe

authors.bio: Norifumi Egami received B.E. and M.E. degrees from Kyushu Institute of Technology in 1987 and 1980, respectively, and a Ph.D. degree from Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan in 2003. In 1980, he joined NHK and worked at the Tokushima regional broadcasting station as a television engineer until 1983. Since 1983, he has been engaged in the research and development of highly sensitive image sensors in the NHK Science and Technology Research Laboratories. Since 2013, he has been a professor in the department of electrical and communication engineering, faculty of humanity-oriented science and engineering at Kinki University, Fukuoka, Japan.
authors.name: Norifumi Egami

authors.bio: Shoji Kawahito received a Ph.D. degree from Tohoku University in 1988 and joined Tohoku University as a Research Associate. From 1989 to 1999, he worked at Toyohashi University of Technology. From 1996 to 1997, he was a visiting professor at ETH, Zurich. Since 1999, he has been a professor at the Research Institute of Electronics, Shizuoka University. In 2006, he became chief technology officer at Brookman Technology, Inc. His research interests are in CMOS imaging devices and mixed-signal sensor interface circuits. He has published more than 250 papers in refereed journals and international conference proceedings. Kawahito has received several awards, including the Beatrice Winner Award for Editorial Excellence at the 2005 IEEE-ISSCC, the 2010 IEICE Electronics Society Award, and the 24th Takayanagi Memorial Award in 2010. He is a Fellow of the IEEE and ITE and a member of the IEICE and SPIE.
authors.name: Shoji Kawahito

authors.bio: Tomohiko Kosugi received a B.S. degree from Chubu University in 2002. He worked at Sanei Hytechs Co., Ltd. from 2002 to 2009, where he was engaged in the design of analog circuit. In 2010, he joined Brookman Technology, Inc., where he has been working on the development and design of CMOS image sensor and analog circuits.
authors.name: Tomohiko Kosugi

authors.bio: Takashi Watanabe received B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. degrees in physics from Osaka University, Japan, in 1974, 1976, and 2000, respectively. He joined Sharp Corporation in 1976. Watanabe worked to develop CCD signal processing ICs, linear image sensors, and area image sensors and also led the development of CMOS image sensors and was involved with the first application to mobile phones in 2000. He was also involved in developing log-type imagers and range image sensors. Since December 2007, he has been with Brookman Technology, Inc. Since April 2011, he has been a visiting professor at the Research Institute of Electronics, Shizuoka University. Watanabe's research interests are CCD and CMOS image sensor device technologies. He holds 145 Japanese patent applications and 48 U.S. patents. Watanabe is a member of the IEEE and the Institute of the Image Information and Television Engineers.
authors.name: Takashi Watanabe

authors.bio: Taku Tsukamoto joined Astrodesign, Inc., in 2000, where he has been engaged in the research and development of digital signal processing for picture quality optimization. He received a M.E. degree in information science from the Nara Institute of Science and Technology in 2000.
authors.name: Taku Tsukamoto
